list.listitem: Patients who are older than 70 years, who have a neurological deficit, or lack vertigo should be investigated for a serious cause of dizziness (medication related, neurologic, or cardiac). C
Perform the Dix-Hallpike maneuver in patients with signs or symptoms of a peripheral vestibular disorder. C

In patients with peripheral vertigo, determine whether symptoms are episodic or persistent, and whether hearing loss is present or absent, to diagnose benign paroxysmal positional vertigo, vestibular neuronitis, labyrinthitis, or Meniere's disease. C
No routine tests are indicated in the diagnosis of dizziness, but check glucose levels in diabetic patients and monitor cardiac rhythm in patients older than 45 years. C
Magnetic resonance imaging is preferred when neuroimaging is indicated in patients with dizziness. C

background.definition: Dizziness is a disturbance in a person's sense of relationship to space, typified by a sensation of unsteadiness and a feeling of movement occurring within the head.

list.listitem: Benign paroxysmal positional vertigo: 64/100,000/year and the incidence increases by 38% with each decade of life.
The mean age at diagnosis is 51 years.
The lifetime prevalence of dizziness is 23% in all adults, and 34% in adults 60 years and older.
The percentage of patients presenting to primary care physicians with dizziness increases from 0.2% in patients up to 14 years old to 6.7% in patients aged 85 years and over.
Approximately 4% of patients with dizziness experience persistent symptoms, and about 3% are severely incapacitated by their symptoms.

A prospective cohort study followed 417 older adults (mean age 79 years) for up to 10 years. Mortality was higher for those with dizziness caused by cardiovascular causes. The vertigo subtype of dizziness had lower mortality.
Peripheral vestibular disorders (35%-55%), including benign positional paroxysmal vertigo, vestibular neuronitis, labyrinthitis, Meniere's disease, perilymphatic fistula.
Psychiatric illness, including anxiety disorders (particularly panic) and depression. Psychiatric illness is the only cause in 9% of patients and is at least contributory in up to 25%.
Central vestibular disorders, including cerebrovascular ischemia or infarction, usually vertebrobasilar (5%); tumor (<1%), especially acoustic neuroma; migraine; and multiple sclerosis.

Presyncope (2%-16%), mostly caused by postural changes with or without orthostatic hypotension from dehydration or autonomic nerve dysfunction; less commonly caused by underlying cardiovascular disease, such as arrhythmias.
Dysequilibrium (1%-15%), usually caused by a combination of sensory deficits (visual impairment, neuropathy, vestibular disorders, musculoskeletal disturbances), especially in older patients.
Prescription drug toxicity (2%-10%).

Less common causes include substance abuse, metabolic abnormalities, hepatic encephalopathy, electrolyte disturbances, systemic and upper respiratory infections, hypertension, trauma, anemia, Alzheimer's disease, Parkinson's disease, seizures, and endocrine disorders.
Multiple diagnoses are common, especially in older patients.

Most common causes in children incluse otitis media, chronic middle ear effusion, and eustachian tube dysfunction. Less common causes: benign paroxysmal positional vertigo of childhood, migraine, trauma, vestibular neuronitis, and Meniere's disease.
From 10% to 25% of cases remain undiagnosed.
Varies according to the underlying condition(s).
Benign paroxysmal positional vertigo is caused by an otolith that stimulates the sense organ in a semicircular canal, producing a false sense of motion.
Vestibular neuronitis and labyrinthitis are usually caused by viral infections involving the vestibular nerve and semicircular canals, respectively.
Meniere's disease involves swelling of the endolymphatic sac, which controls the filtration and excretion of fluid in the semicircular canals, but the exact cause of the disease is unknown.
Perilymphatic fistulas are leaks of endolymph from the vestibular apparatus caused by trauma, barotrauma, or excessive straining.
Ototoxic medications damage the vestibular apparatus and cause bilateral peripheral vestibular disorders.

Cerebrovascular and cardiovascular diseases causing dizziness compromise cerebral blood flow, particularly through the vertebrobasilar system, which supplies blood to areas of the brain that control balance and coordination.

Differential.Differential_Features: Brief episodes of intense vertigo with changes in head position
Severe vertigo for several hours to days, nausea/vomiting, usually viral
Symptoms of vestibular neuronitis with tinnitus and/or hearing loss
Episodic vertigo lasting hours, sensorineural hearing loss, tinnitus, ear fullness
Focal neurological findings, headache, numbness/weakness/tingling, ataxia
Throbbing unilateral headache with or without aura
Worsening symptoms when upright, positive orthostatic measurements
Panic attacks, constant worry or stress, sleep disturbance
Sadness, anhedonia, psychomotor retardation, sleep and/or appetite disturbance

Differential.Differential_Name: Cardiovascular disease (arryhthmia, acute coronary syndrome, pericarditis)
Differential.Differential_Features: Syncope, lightheadedness, pallor, worse with prolonged standing, cardiovascular risk factors

Vertigo and hearing loss after traumatic event (direct blow to head, barotrauma, loud noise, excessive straining), positive Hennebert's sign (vertigo/nystagmus induced by pressure on tragus and external auditory canal)

Differential.Differential_Name: Autonomic dysregulation (orthostatic hypotension, postural orthostatic tachycardia syndrome, neurocardiogenic syncope)
Differential.Differential_Features: Symptoms triggered or worse when upright, lightheadedness, presyncope or syncope, positive Schellong sign or tilt table test

list.listitem: Older age (over 70 years), neurological deficit, or lack of vertigo predicts a serious cause of dizziness with 86% sensitivity. Potential serious causes of dizziness include adverse effect of medication; central nervous system disease, such as seizure or cerebrovascular episode (stroke, transient ischemic attack, vertebrobasilar insufficiency); and cardiovascular disease (arrhythmia, hypertension, pericarditis).

In patients with dizziness, the combination of nausea or vomiting and a positive Dix-Hallpike maneuver (see ) result is strong evidence in favor of peripheral vestibular disorder, but a negative Dix-Hallpike maneuver result does not rule it out.

In patients with peripheral vertigo, a strategy using the presence or absence of hearing loss and whether vertigo was episodic or persistent correctly diagnosed benign paroxysmal positional vertigo, vestibular neuronitis, labyrinthitis, or Meniere's disease 60% of the time (see ).
Patients who associate dizziness with panic attacks report higher rates of vertigo, fainting, agoraphobic behavior, and occupational disability than those who had no dizziness with panic attacks.

In patients with vertigo, the Dix-Hallpike maneuver (also called the Nylen-Barany test) has an 83% positive predictive value for benign paroxysmal positional vertigo, but its negative predictive value is only 52% (see ).
Nystagmus caused by a peripheral vestibular disorder is often suppressed by visual fixation, but may be detected during funduscopic examination in the dark.

Orthostatic measurements are most useful in detecting moderate or severe dehydration. However, there is a wide range of normal for orthostatic blood pressure and pulse measurements. Approximately 50% of elderly patients have positive orthostatic measurements, but they may not be reproducible.

In patients with acute vertigo, a systematic review identified nystagmus type (bidirectional, vertical, direction changing, or pure torsional nystagmus) and an abnormal test of skew as the best physical exam findings for stroke as the cause of vertigo. Nystagmus type, test of skew, and signs of dysmetria were the best predictors of any central cause for acute vertigo.
The Weber and Rinne tests and the Dix-Hallpike maneuver may not be as useful in older patients.
Carotid sinus massage has low yield in identifying patients with significant arrhythmias (6% in patients older than 60 years with unexplained dizziness).

In patients with orthostatic symptoms, the Schellong test can be useful in identifying patients with postural orthostatic tachycardia or neurocardiogenic syncope. This test is helpful when positive but does not rule out the diagnosis if negative.

Several qualitative vestibular physical exam tests have been described to diagnose peripheral vestibular disorders (see ); however, there is no evidence regarding the sensitivity and specificity of these tests compared with quantitative vestibular testing techniques (see below).

Among 881 patients presenting to the emergency department with presyncope (defined as a feeling of impending loss of consciousness without lost consciousness, and excluding patients with mental status changes, seizures or significant trauma) the prevalance of serious outcomes (defined as death, arrhythmia, MI, pulmonary embolism or hemorrhage) in the overall population was 5.1% at 30 days, and 1.9% among those discharged home.

Acute vestibular syndrome (AVS) is characterized by acute, spontaneous, persistent (lasts days to weeks) dizziness; nausea or vomiting and nystagmus; head motion intolerance and gait unsteadiness. The HINTS examination is helpful in differentiating peripheral from central etiologies when used among trained clinicians (see ).

No routine testing is indicated for all patients with dizziness. Check glucose levels in diabetic patients (to diagnose reactive hypoglycemia). Monitor cardiac rhythm in patients older than 45 years. Certain low yield tests may be performed in a directed manner, when indicated (see ).

Consider neuroimaging studies if exam suggests patient has: central nervous system or invasive otologic disease; acute vertigo and high risk for cerebrovascular disease, based on age and risk factors; or progressive hearing loss with abnormal speech reception thresholds.

MRI of the brain is preferred over computed tomography when indicated in patients with sensorineural hearing loss and acute or intermittent vertigo, and in patients with acute vertigo but without hearing loss or neurological findings. Both brain MRI and magnetic resonance angiography of the head may be useful in patients with new-onset episodic vertigo lasting hours to days.

In one series of patients with dizziness referred for brain MRI or head CT, relevant abnormal findings were found by CT in 29% of patients and by MRI in 40%. Overall, 34% of patients had relevant abnormal findings, the most common of which were atrophy, infarction, and demyelination.
Audiometry may distinguish Meniere's disease from migraine-associated vertigo.

When ordering arrhythmia monitoring to diagnose dizziness, patient-triggered event recorders with continuous automatic arrhythmia detection are superior to 24-hour Holter monitoring or patient-triggered event recorders alone. Around-the-clock Holter monitoring will miss more than half of relevant arrhythmias, and patient-triggered event recorders capture only approximately one sixth of clinically relevant arrhythmias.

If a vestibular disorder is suspected but not confirmed by the clinical examination, consider a neurology, neurotology, or otolaryngology referral for further vestibular testing with quantitative techniques such as electronystagmography or infrared video oculography with caloric irrigation or passive rotational testing.

In an article involving 23 studies and 15,721 patients, the sensitivity and specificity for identifying acute cerebrovascular events in the emergency department was 91.3% and 92.7%; however the risk of misdiagnosis was highest in patients presenting with nonspecific or transient symptoms such as dizziness.
History alone leads to a diagnosis in approximately 75% of patients.
See algorithm in for the recommended diagnostic strategy.

feature.caption: Qualitative Clinical Vestibular Tests.
feature.feature_body:
Name Description
Dix-Hallpike (aka, Nylan-Barany) maneuver Patient starts in sitting position with head turned 45 degrees toward the affected side, then lies down with head hanging at about 30 degrees; reproduction of symptoms after 2-20 seconds suggests vestibular lesion.
Schellong test Patient stands for 10-20 minutes while blood pressure is measured continuously; a fall of systolic pressure of 20 mm Hg or more indicates poor circulatory function.
Subjective visual vertical Patient perceives vertical as 10-30 degrees tilted toward affected side shortly after unilateral vestibular loss; usually diminishes with time.
Head-shaking nystagmus Patient closes eyes, turns head back and forth horizontally for about 30 seconds, then stops and opens eyes; nystagmus beats away from affected side; no such nystagmus in normal subjects.
Head thrust Catch-up saccade when head is turned rapidly toward affected side.
Vibration-induced nystagmus The examiner either taps the patient's head or applies a 60-Hz vibration stimulus to mastoid bone; causes horizontal nystagmus beating away from affected side.
Dynamic visual acuity testing Patient has visual acuity tested at baseline with head still, then tested again while turning head from side to side at 1 Hz or more; a worsening of visual acuity by 3 lines or more on visual acuity chart suggests bilateral vestibular loss.
Hyperventilation Accentuates downbeating nystagmus in patients with cerebellar lesions; causes nystagmus toward affected side in some patients with vestibular schwannoma.
Data from Fife TD, Tusa RJ, Furman JM, et al. Assessment: vestibular testing techniques in adults and children: report of the Therapeutics and Technology Assessment Subcommittee of the American Academy of Neurology. Neurology 2000;55:1431–1441.

May be abnormal in patients with psychogenic dizziness

Consistent with a central cause of dizziness

tr.td: Patient looks straight ahead; hold skull; quick movements lateral → midline
“Catch up” saccade toward the normal side
Patient looks straight ahead; then to the right & left; (Note the direction of the fast component – fast component to the left = left beating nystagmus, & vice versa)
Nystagmus never changes direction – always beating in a single horizontal plane (unidirectional – left beating OR right beating nystagmus)
When looking to the side where the nystagmus is less intense – nystagmus reverses direction (bidirectional - – left beating AND right beating nystagmus); or vertical or torsional
Patient looks straight ahead; Alternately cover and uncover each eye
No vertical deviation of either eye
